claim: The gain-of-function mutation in the TALK-1 K+ channel (p.L114P) is associated with maturity-onset diabetes of the young (MODY).
source: The gain-of-function mutation in the TALK-1 K+ channel (p.L114P) is associated with maturity-onset diabetes of the young (MODY).
evidence: This is the central claim of the study, supported by the generation and characterization of a mouse model and referenced to prior work (Graff et al., 2021).

claim: Heterozygous and homozygous Kcnk16 L114P mice exhibit increased neonatal lethality in the C57BL/6J and the CD-1 (ICR) genetic background, respectively.
source: Heterozygous and homozygous Kcnk16 L114P mice exhibit increased neonatal lethality in the C57BL/6J and the CD-1 (ICR) genetic background, respectively.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data showing survival rates in different genetic backgrounds.

claim: Neonatal lethality in Kcnk16 L114P mice is likely a result of severe hyperglycemia due to lack of glucose-stimulated insulin secretion.
source: Lethality is likely a result of severe hyperglycemia observed in the homozygous Kcnk16 L114P neonates due to lack of glucose-stimulated insulin secretion and can be reduced with insulin treatment.
evidence: This claim is supported by measurements of blood glucose, insulin levels, and the rescue effect of insulin treatment shown in the data.

claim: Insulin treatment can reduce neonatal lethality in Kcnk16 L114P mice.
source: Lethality is likely a result of severe hyperglycemia observed in the homozygous Kcnk16 L114P neonates due to lack of glucose-stimulated insulin secretion and can be reduced with insulin treatment.
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally by survival curves showing extended lifespan with insulin treatment.

claim: Kcnk16 L114P increased whole-cell β-cell K+ currents resulting in blunted glucose-stimulated Ca2+ entry.
source: Kcnk16 L114P increased whole-cell β-cell K+ currents resulting in blunted glucose-stimulated Ca2+ entry and loss of glucose-induced Ca2+ oscillations.
evidence: This is supported by patch-clamp electrophysiology data and calcium imaging experiments.

claim: Kcnk16 L114P causes loss of glucose-induced Ca2+ oscillations.
source: Kcnk16 L114P increased whole-cell β-cell K+ currents resulting in blunted glucose-stimulated Ca2+ entry and loss of glucose-induced Ca2+ oscillations.
evidence: This is demonstrated by calcium imaging data showing absence of oscillations in mutant islets.

claim: Adult Kcnk16 L114P mice have reduced glucose-stimulated insulin secretion and plasma insulin levels.
source: Thus, adult Kcnk16 L114P mice have reduced glucose-stimulated insulin secretion and plasma insulin levels, which significantly impairs glucose homeostasis.
evidence: This is supported by insulin secretion assays and plasma insulin measurements in adult mice.

claim: Adult Kcnk16 L114P mice have significantly impaired glucose homeostasis.
source: Thus, adult Kcnk16 L114P mice have reduced glucose-stimulated insulin secretion and plasma insulin levels, which significantly impairs glucose homeostasis.
evidence: This is demonstrated by glucose tolerance tests showing impaired glucose clearance.

claim: The MODY-associated Kcnk16 L114P mutation disrupts glucose homeostasis in adult mice resembling a MODY phenotype.
source: Taken together, this study shows that the MODY-associated Kcnk16 L114P mutation disrupts glucose homeostasis in adult mice resembling a MODY phenotype and causes neonatal lethality by inhibiting islet insulin secretion during development.
evidence: This is the main conclusion supported by multiple experimental findings including glucose tolerance tests and insulin secretion measurements.

claim: The Kcnk16 L114P mutation causes neonatal lethality by inhibiting islet insulin secretion during development.
source: Taken together, this study shows that the MODY-associated Kcnk16 L114P mutation disrupts glucose homeostasis in adult mice resembling a MODY phenotype and causes neonatal lethality by inhibiting islet insulin secretion during development.
evidence: This is supported by data showing loss of glucose-stimulated insulin secretion in neonatal islets and rescue with insulin treatment.

claim: TALK-1 is an islet-restricted target for the treatment for diabetes.
source: These data suggest that TALK-1 is an islet-restricted target for the treatment for diabetes.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the islet-specific expression and functional role of TALK-1 demonstrated in the study.

claim: Mutations in 15 genes involved in β-cell development and function have been associated with MODY.
source: To date, mutations in 15 genes involved in β-cell development and function have been associated with MODY (Broome et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review article.

claim: Monogenic diabetes cases account for approximately 1–5% of the total diabetic patient population.
source: Monogenic diabetes cases account for approximately 1–5% of the total diabetic patient population (Kavvoura and Owen, 2012; Zhang et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous epidemiological studies.

claim: Many MODY patients are misdiagnosed because the phenotype overlaps with other forms of diabetes.
source: However, as the phenotype of MODY overlaps with other forms of diabetes, many patients are misdiagnosed (Shields et al., 2010; Greeley et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical studies.

claim: In the US, ~70% of registered monogenic diabetes cases do not have a known genetic cause.
source: Data from monogenic diabetes registries also suggests that in the US, ~70% of the registered cases still do not have a known genetic cause, and similarly many patients in the UK (~50%) with monogenic diabetes have MODY-causing mutations that remain to be determined (Bowden et al., 2021; Shepherd et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to registry data.

claim: In the UK, ~50% of patients with monogenic diabetes have MODY-causing mutations that remain to be determined.
source: Data from monogenic diabetes registries also suggests that in the US, ~70% of the registered cases still do not have a known genetic cause, and similarly many patients in the UK (~50%) with monogenic diabetes have MODY-causing mutations that remain to be determined (Bowden et al., 2021; Shepherd et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to registry data.

claim: Some MODY-associated mutations are only reported in single families and require genetic and mechanistic confirmation.
source: Additionally, some MODY-associated mutations are only reported in single families, and thus require genetic and mechanistic confirmation (Yamagata et al., 1996; Pearson et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to case reports.

claim: A mutation in KCNK16 (p. Kcnk16 L114P) co-segregates with MODY in a four-generation family.
source: We recently identified a mutation in KCNK16, the gene encoding TALK-1 channels (p. Kcnk16 L114P), which co-segregates with MODY in a four-generation family (Graff et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous genetic study.

claim: KCNK16 is the most islet-restricted and abundant β-cell K+ channel transcript.
source: As KCNK16 is the most islet-restricted and abundant β-cell K+ channel transcript, the Kcnk16 L114P mutation is likely to perturb β-cell function and cause MODY (Bramswig et al., 2013; Blodgett et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to transcriptomic studies.

claim: A Japanese family with the identical KCNK16 mutation (p. Kcnk16 L114P) segregating with MODY was recently reported.
source: This was further strengthened by a recent report of a Japanese family with the identical KCNK16 mutation (p. Kcnk16 L114P) segregating with MODY (Katsuyuki Matsui et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a recent case report.

claim: TALK-1 is a key regulator of β-cell membrane potential (Vm), glucose-stimulated Ca2+ influx, and insulin secretion.
source: TALK-1 is a key regulator of β-cell membrane potential (Vm), glucose-stimulated Ca2+ influx, and insulin secretion (Vierra et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous functional study.

claim: A non-synonymous gain-of-function polymorphism in KCNK16 (rs1535500; p. Kcnk16 A277E) is associated with an increased risk for type 2 diabetes (T2D).
source: A non-synonymous gain-of-function polymorphism in KCNK16 (rs1535500; p. Kcnk16 A277E) is also associated with an increased risk for type 2 diabetes (T2D) (Cho et al., 2011; Mahajan et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to genome-wide association studies.

claim: The MODY-associated Kcnk16 L114P mutation results in a significant gain-of-function in TALK-1 K+ flux.
source: Moreover, we recently determined that the MODY-associated Kcnk16 L114P mutation results in a significant gain-of-function in TALK-1 K+ flux (Graff et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous functional characterization study.

claim: When heterologously expressed in β-cells, TALK-1 L114P inhibited glucose-stimulated membrane potential (Vm) depolarization and Ca2+ influx in most β-cells.
source: Interestingly, when heterologously expressed in β-cells, TALK-1 L114P inhibited glucose-stimulated membrane potential (Vm) depolarization and Ca2+ influx in most β-cells.
evidence: This is based on previous experimental data from heterologous expression studies.

claim: TALK-1 L114P-mediated changes in inhibition of electrical activity and Ca2+ influx resulted in only partial blunting of β-cell insulin secretion.
source: Although TALK-1 L114P-mediated changes in inhibition of electrical activity and Ca2+ influx would be predicted to fully inhibit glucose-stimulated insulin secretion, they only resulted in partial blunting of β-cell insulin secretion.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations from heterologous expression studies.

claim: Kcnk16 L114P MODY patients required low-dose insulin therapy.
source: However, this is consistent with Kcnk16 L114P MODY patients that required low-dose insulin therapy which also suggested that this mutation does not fully suppress glucose-stimulated insulin secretion.
evidence: This is based on clinical data from MODY patients with this mutation.

claim: Inhibition of β-cell Ca2+ influx with K+ channel pharmacological activation or gain-of-function mutations (e.g. KATP R201H) results in complete inhibition of glucose-stimulated insulin secretion.
source: This differs from previous studies showing that inhibition of β-cell Ca2+ influx with either K+ channel pharmacological activation or gain-of-function mutations (e.g. KATP R201H) results in complete inhibition of glucose-stimulated insulin secretion (Gloyn et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study on KATP mutations.

claim: TALK-1 is expressed in δ-cells where its activity limits somatostatin secretion.
source: For example, TALK-1 is also expressed in δ-cells where its activity limits somatostatin secretion (Vierra et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study on TALK-1 function in δ-cells.

claim: Somatostatin exerts inhibitory tone on islet β- and α-cells.
source: Because somatostatin exerts inhibitory tone on islet β- and α-cells, TALK-1 L114P-mediated reductions in δ-cell somatostatin secretion would be predicted to increase both glucagon and insulin secretion.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of somatostatin's paracrine effects in islets.

claim: TALK-1 L114P-mediated reductions in δ-cell somatostatin secretion would be predicted to increase both glucagon and insulin secretion.
source: Because somatostatin exerts inhibitory tone on islet β- and α-cells, TALK-1 L114P-mediated reductions in δ-cell somatostatin secretion would be predicted to increase both glucagon and insulin secretion.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the known inhibitory role of somatostatin.

claim: KATP is the only ion channel besides TALK-1 to be linked to MODY.
source: KATP is the only ion channel besides TALK-1 to be linked to MODY; this is due to mutations in genes encoding the KATP channel complex (KCNJ11 and ABCC8) or mutations in genes affecting ATP synthesis (e.g. glucokinase) (Bonnefond et al., 2012; Huopio et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous genetic studies.

claim: MODY-associated mutations in KCNJ11 and ABCC8 have been found to cause permanent or transient neonatal diabetes, and late-onset diabetes.
source: Interestingly, MODY-associated mutations in KCNJ11 and ABCC8 have also been found to cause other diabetic phenotypes including permanent or transient neonatal diabetes, and late-onset diabetes (Yorifuji et al., 2005; Devaraja et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical studies.

claim: Depolarization-dependent activation (outward rectification) of TALK-1 currents may limit the activity of TALK-1 L114P channels at resting Vm.
source: For example, depolarization-dependent activation (outward rectification) of TALK-1 currents may limit the activity of TALK-1 L114P channels at resting Vm (Girard et al., 2001).
evidence: This is based on citation to a previous biophysical characterization study and represents an inference about the mutation's effects.

claim: KATP channels show larger unitary conductance than TALK-1.
source: KATP channels also show larger unitary conductance than TALK-1, not much voltage dependence, and are nucleotide gated (Rorsman and Ashcroft, 2018; Kang and Kim, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to biophysical studies.

claim: KATP channels show not much voltage dependence and are nucleotide gated.
source: KATP channels also show larger unitary conductance than TALK-1, not much voltage dependence, and are nucleotide gated (Rorsman and Ashcroft, 2018; Kang and Kim, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to biophysical studies.

claim: Heterozygous Kcnk16 L114P (L/P) mice exhibited neonatal lethality in the C57BL/6J background as indicated by extremely low number at weaning.
source: Surprisingly, heterozygous Kcnk16 L114P (L/P) mice exhibited neonatal lethality as indicated by extremely low number of Kcnk16 L114P (L/P) mice at weaning (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by chi-square analysis of genotype ratios at weaning shown in Figure 1B.

claim: In the mixed B6;CD-1 background, neonatal lethality was observed in the homozygous B6;CD-1 Kcnk16 L114P (P/P) mice on ~postnatal day 4 (P4), but not in the heterozygous B6;CD-1 Kcnk16 L114P (L/P) mice.
source: Intriguingly, in the mixed background, neonatal lethality was observed in the homozygous B6;CD-1 Kcnk16 L114P (P/P) mice on ~postnatal day 4 (P4), but not in the heterozygous B6;CD-1 Kcnk16 L114P (L/P) mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by survival data and genotype ratios shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: Lethality in Kcnk16 L114P mice was likely independent of growth defects as body weight did not differ between genotypes.
source: Lethality was likely independent of growth defects as body weight did not differ between genotypes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by body weight measurements shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: Heterozygous and homozygous Kcnk16 L114P neonates showed severe hyperglycemia on P4 compared to control littermates.
source: Heterozygous and homozygous Kcnk16 L114P neonates showed severe hyperglycemia and a concurrent reduction in plasma insulin levels in a gene dosage-dependent manner compared to the control littermates (WT) on P4 (Figure 1C and D, and Figure 1—figure supplements 1E and 2A, B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by blood glucose measurements shown in Figure 1C and supplementary figures.

claim: Heterozygous and homozygous Kcnk16 L114P neonates showed a concurrent reduction in plasma insulin levels in a gene dosage-dependent manner on P4.
source: Heterozygous and homozygous Kcnk16 L114P neonates showed severe hyperglycemia and a concurrent reduction in plasma insulin levels in a gene dosage-dependent manner compared to the control littermates (WT) on P4 (Figure 1C and D, and Figure 1—figure supplements 1E and 2A, B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by plasma insulin measurements shown in Figure 1D and supplementary figures.

claim: Hyperglycemia in neonatal Kcnk16 L114P mice subsided by P10, when glycemia was equivalent to WT controls.
source: Hyperglycemia in neonatal Kcnk16 L114P mice subsided by P10, when glycemia was equivalent to WT controls (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by blood glucose measurements over time shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: The Kcnk16 L114P mutation blunted glucose-stimulated insulin secretion in P4 islets from heterozygous neonates and decreased it further in P4 islets from homozygous neonates.
source: Additionally, the Kcnk16 L114P mutation blunted glucose-stimulated insulin secretion in P4 islets from heterozygous neonates and decreased it further in P4 islets from homozygous neonates (Figure 1E and F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vitro insulin secretion assays shown in Figure 1E and F.

claim: Changes in glucose-stimulated insulin secretion and glucose homeostasis in Kcnk16 L114P mice are likely not due to altered islet mass as pancreas weight was unchanged.
source: These changes in glucose-stimulated insulin secretion and glucose homeostasis are likely due to TALK-1 L114P channel mediated alteration in islet function and not islet mass as pancreas weight was unchanged (Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by pancreas weight measurements shown in Figure 1G and supplementary figure.

claim: Neonatal islet composition was unaltered except for a modest increase in the α-cell (glucagon+) area/islet in the Kcnk16 L114P (L/P) pancreas.
source: Furthermore, neonatal islet composition was unaltered except for a modest increase in the α-cell (glucagon+) area/islet in the Kcnk16 L114P (L/P) pancreas (Figure 1H–J).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunostaining and quantification shown in Figure 1H-J.

claim: Kcnk16 L114P (L/P and P/P) neonatal islets exhibited a complete lack of glucose-stimulated Ca2+ entry.
source: The loss of glucose-stimulated insulin secretion can be explained by a complete lack of glucose-stimulated Ca2+ entry in islets from Kcnk16 L114P (L/P and P/P) neonates (Figure 1K–N).
evidence: This is demonstrated by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 1K-N.

claim: Kcnk16 L114P (L/P and P/P) neonatal islets exhibited KCl-mediated β-cell Vm depolarization-induced Ca2+ entry.
source: However, these islets exhibited KCl-mediated β-cell Vm depolarization-induced Ca2+ entry; this indicates that TALK-1 L114P channels hyperpolarize β-cell Vm, thereby overriding the effect of KATP closure due to glucose metabolism and lead to insufficient glucose-stimulated insulin secretion and hyperglycemia.
evidence: This is demonstrated by calcium imaging with KCl stimulation shown in Figure 1K-N.

claim: TALK-1 L114P channels hyperpolarize β-cell Vm, thereby overriding the effect of KATP closure due to glucose metabolism.
source: However, these islets exhibited KCl-mediated β-cell Vm depolarization-induced Ca2+ entry; this indicates that TALK-1 L114P channels hyperpolarize β-cell Vm, thereby overriding the effect of KATP closure due to glucose metabolism and lead to insufficient glucose-stimulated insulin secretion and hyperglycemia.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that KCl can rescue Ca2+ entry but glucose cannot.

claim: Insulin treatment (Glargine Lantus; 0.2 U/kg/day, once-daily subcutaneous injection) was able to extend the lifespan of Kcnk16 L114P (P/P) neonates.
source: Importantly, insulin treatment (Glargine Lantus; 0.2 U/kg/day, once-daily subcutaneous injection) was able to extend the lifespan of Kcnk16 L114P (P/P) neonates, suggesting lethality results from hyperglycemia due to inadequate insulin secretion (Figure 1O).
evidence: This is demonstrated by survival curves shown in Figure 1O.

claim: Male Kcnk16 L114P (L/P) mice developed glucose intolerance as early as 11 weeks of age in the B6;CD-1 background and 8 weeks of age in the B6 background.
source: Male Kcnk16 L114P (L/P) mice developed glucose intolerance as early as 11 weeks of age in the B6;CD-1 background and 8 weeks of age in the B6 background compared to their respective control littermates (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from glucose tolerance tests.

claim: Male B6;CD-1 Kcnk16 L114P (L/P) mice developed impaired oral glucose tolerance by 7 weeks of age.
source: Similarly, male B6;CD-1 Kcnk16 L114P (L/P) mice developed impaired oral glucose tolerance by 7 weeks of age (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by oral glucose tolerance test data shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: The defect in glucose homeostasis is maintained with age in the male Kcnk16 L114P (L/P) mice.
source: This defect in glucose homeostasis is maintained with age in the male Kcnk16 L114P (L/P) mice (Figure 2A–C and Figure 2—figure supplements 1A–C and 2A–C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by glucose tolerance tests at multiple ages shown in Figure 2 and supplementary figures.

claim: Male Kcnk16 L114P (L/P) mice exhibit fasting hyperglycemia.
source: Furthermore, male Kcnk16 L114P (L/P) mice also exhibit fasting hyperglycemia indicating a likely non-β-cell-specific islet defect in this mouse model (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by fasting blood glucose measurements shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Fasting hyperglycemia in male Kcnk16 L114P (L/P) mice indicates a likely non-β-cell-specific islet defect.
source: Furthermore, male Kcnk16 L114P (L/P) mice also exhibit fasting hyperglycemia indicating a likely non-β-cell-specific islet defect in this mouse model (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of fasting hyperglycemia, which suggests involvement of glucagon secretion.

claim: There were no body weight differences in male Kcnk16 L114P (L/P) mice compared to controls.
source: There were no body weight differences in males (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by body weight measurements shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Female Kcnk16 L114P (L/P) mice only developed moderate glucose intolerance compared to the controls (WT) in both B6 and B6;CD-1 genetic backgrounds.
source: Female Kcnk16 L114P (L/P) mice only developed moderate glucose intolerance compared to the controls (WT) in both B6 and B6;CD-1 genetic backgrounds (Figure 2E–G; Figure 2—figure supplement 1D–F, 2E, F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by glucose tolerance test data shown in Figure 2E-G and supplementary figures.

claim: The Kcnk16 L114P mutation resulted in greater body weight gain in B6;CD-1 females compared to the WT controls.
source: Moreover, the Kcnk16 L114P mutation resulted in greater body weight gain in B6;CD-1 females compared to the WT controls (Figure 2H) due to increased lean mass, which might reduce glucose intolerance in Kcnk16 L114P (L/P) females compared to males (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A–F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by body weight and body composition measurements shown in Figure 2H and supplementary figure.

claim: Increased body weight in female Kcnk16 L114P (L/P) mice was due to increased lean mass.
source: Moreover, the Kcnk16 L114P mutation resulted in greater body weight gain in B6;CD-1 females compared to the WT controls (Figure 2H) due to increased lean mass, which might reduce glucose intolerance in Kcnk16 L114P (L/P) females compared to males (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A–F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by body composition analysis shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: Increased lean mass might reduce glucose intolerance in Kcnk16 L114P (L/P) females compared to males.
source: Moreover, the Kcnk16 L114P mutation resulted in greater body weight gain in B6;CD-1 females compared to the WT controls (Figure 2H) due to increased lean mass, which might reduce glucose intolerance in Kcnk16 L114P (L/P) females compared to males (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A–F).
evidence: This is a speculative inference about the relationship between lean mass and glucose tolerance.

claim: The T2D-associated SNP in KCNK16 (rs1535500) which causes gain-of-function in TALK-1 activity has shown a significant association with increased total cholesterol in a Han Chinese population.
source: The T2D-associated SNP in KCNK16 (rs1535500) which causes gain-of-function in TALK-1 activity has shown a significant association with increased total cholesterol in a Han Chinese population (Permana et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous association study.

claim: An increase in TALK-1 activity due to the Kcnk16 L114P mutation did not affect plasma and liver triglyceride and cholesterol levels in mice.
source: However, an increase in TALK-1 activity due to the Kcnk16 L114P mutation did not affect plasma and liver triglyceride and cholesterol levels in mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 3G–J).
evidence: This is demonstrated by lipid measurements shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: Both male and female Kcnk16 L114P (L/P) mice exhibited reduced plasma insulin levels at 15 min and 30 min following an intraperitoneal glucose injection after a 4 hr fast.
source: Both male and female Kcnk16 L114P (L/P) mice exhibited reduced plasma insulin levels compared to controls at 15 min and 30 min following an intraperitoneal glucose injection after a 4 hr fast (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by plasma insulin measurements shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: Insulin sensitivity was not altered in the Kcnk16 L114P (L/P) mice.
source: Insulin sensitivity was not altered in the Kcnk16 L114P (L/P) mice indicating that the reduction in glucose tolerance is primarily due to an islet secretion defect (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by insulin tolerance test data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The reduction in glucose tolerance in Kcnk16 L114P (L/P) mice is primarily due to an islet secretion defect.
source: Insulin sensitivity was not altered in the Kcnk16 L114P (L/P) mice indicating that the reduction in glucose tolerance is primarily due to an islet secretion defect (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is an inference based on normal insulin sensitivity despite glucose intolerance.

claim: Islets from Kcnk16 L114P (L/P) mice exhibited reduced ability to secrete insulin in response to glucose.
source: Islets from Kcnk16 L114P (L/P) mice exhibited reduced ability to secrete insulin in response to glucose and showed elevated glucagon secretion under low glucose (2 mM) and euglycemic (7 mM) conditions (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vitro insulin secretion assays shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Islets from Kcnk16 L114P (L/P) mice showed elevated glucagon secretion under low glucose (2 mM) and euglycemic (7 mM) conditions.
source: Islets from Kcnk16 L114P (L/P) mice exhibited reduced ability to secrete insulin in response to glucose and showed elevated glucagon secretion under low glucose (2 mM) and euglycemic (7 mM) conditions (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vitro glucagon secretion assays shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The fasting hyperglycemia observed in male Kcnk16 L114P (L/P) mice is likely a result of the observed increase in glucagon secretion under fasting conditions.
source: This indicates that the fasting hyperglycemia observed in male Kcnk16 L114P (L/P) mice (Figure 2B) is likely a result of the observed increase in glucagon secretion under fasting conditions.
evidence: This is an inference connecting elevated glucagon secretion to fasting hyperglycemia.

claim: Kcnk16 L114P (L/P) pancreata showed an increase in glucagon-positive area/islet.
source: Immunostaining analyses revealed an increase in glucagon-positive area/islet and a concurrent modest reduction in insulin-positive area/islet in Kcnk16 L114P (L/P) pancreata (Figure 3F–J).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunostaining and quantification shown in Figure 3F-J.

claim: Kcnk16 L114P (L/P) pancreata showed a concurrent modest reduction in insulin-positive area/islet.
source: Immunostaining analyses revealed an increase in glucagon-positive area/islet and a concurrent modest reduction in insulin-positive area/islet in Kcnk16 L114P (L/P) pancreata (Figure 3F–J).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunostaining and quantification shown in Figure 3F-J.

claim: Kcnk16 L114P mutation leads to disruptions in both islet composition and secretion giving rise to a MODY-like phenotype in adult mice.
source: Together, these results indicate that Kcnk16 L114P mutation leads to disruptions in both islet composition and secretion giving rise to a MODY-like phenotype in adult mice.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on multiple experimental findings.

claim: Perforated patch-clamp recordings revealed blunting of β-cell Vm depolarization and loss of action potential firing in islets from Kcnk16 L114P (L/P) mice.
source: Perforated patch-clamp recordings revealed blunting of β-cell Vm depolarization and loss of action potential firing in islets from Kcnk16 L114P (L/P) mice (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: Kcnk16 L114P β-cells showed blunted glucose-stimulated Vm depolarization, which did not reach a depolarized threshold to fire action potentials in 67% of β-cells.
source: Similar to the whole islet recordings, Kcnk16 L114P β-cells showed blunted glucose-stimulated Vm depolarization, which did not reach a depolarized threshold to fire action potentials in 67% of β-cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiology recordings from individual β-cells shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: 33% of Kcnk16 L114P β-cells showed glucose-stimulated action potential firing, indicating that these cells may also undergo Ca2+ entry and glucose-stimulated insulin secretion.
source: However, as 33% of Kcnk16 L114P β-cells showed glucose-stimulated action potential firing (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), this indicates that these cells may also undergo Ca2+ entry and glucose-stimulated insulin secretion.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that some β-cells retain electrical activity.

claim: Reduced glucose-stimulated islet Vm depolarization and action potential firing in Kcnk16 L114P β-cells was in part a result of increased whole-cell two-pore domain K+ channel currents at depolarized Vm.
source: Reduced glucose-stimulated islet Vm depolarization and action potential firing in Kcnk16 L114P β-cells was in part a result of increased whole-cell two-pore domain K+ channel currents at depolarized Vm and thus reducing K+ channel activity with high KCl depolarized these cells (Figure 4C and D; Figure 4—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by whole-cell current recordings shown in Figure 4C and D and supplementary figures.

claim: TALK-1 L114P (L/P and P/P) channels did not show a substantial increase at hyperpolarized β-cell membrane potentials under low and high glucose where these K+ currents are typically active.
source: However, TALK-1 L114P (L/P and P/P) channels did not show a substantial increase at hyperpolarized β-cell membrane potentials under low and high glucose where these K+ currents are typically active (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by current-voltage relationship data shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: Overexpression of the mouse mutant TALK-1 L114P channel results in large K+ currents indicative of a similar gain-of-function in mouse TALK-1 current as the human TALK-1 current due to the L114P mutation.
source: Indeed, overexpression of the mouse mutant channel results in large K+ currents indicative of a similar gain-of-function in mouse TALK-1 current as the human TALK-1 current due to the L114P mutation (Figure 4E and F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by whole-cell current recordings from HEK293T cells shown in Figure 4E and F.

claim: TALK-1 L114P blunted islet glucose-stimulated [Ca2+]c influx in mice on both B6 and B6;CD-1 genetic backgrounds compared to WT controls.
source: TALK-1 L114P blunted islet glucose-stimulated [Ca2+]c influx in mice on both B6 and B6;CD-1 genetic backgrounds compared to WT controls (Figure 5A–F and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5A-F and supplementary figure.
